metadata.title: AI semiconductor rout may be buying opportunity, LYNX Equity says: ’Dip a toe in’

content.text:
Investing.com -- Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) shares rebounded sharply in premarket trading Friday after the semiconductor equipment maker announced a $25 billion share repurchase authorization, offering a potential signal of corporate confidence following one of the technology sector's worst trading sessions in years.
Lam shares had plunged 16.4% on Thursday, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) sank 12.25%, its steepest one-day decline since March 2020. The index closed at 9,011.14, as investors aggressively reduced exposure to AI-related stocks amid growing concerns about the sustainability of data-center investment.
The sell-off extended across the semiconductor industry, with Micron (NASDAQ:MU) falling 17.5%, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) losing 17.3% and SanDisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) dropping more than 22%. Lam was among the hardest-hit equipment manufacturers.
The Friday rebound in Lam, which rose approximately 11% premarket to $205.65, came after the company announced that its board had approved the new $25 billion repurchase authorization. The program supplements the remaining balance of its previous authorization and has no termination date.
The announcement also drew attention from LYNX Equity Strategies, with KC Rajkumar arguing that the timing of the buyback could indicate that the semiconductor equipment maker is not experiencing the deterioration in demand implied by the recent share-price decline.
In a research note titled "AI Semis: When There Is Blood on the Streets," Rajkumar said the worst of the sell-off may be behind the sector, suggesting that investors could begin selectively rebuilding positions.
Supply constraints could shield semiconductor suppliers
Rajkumar's central argument is that concerns about AI infrastructure spending should not necessarily be confused with a deterioration in near-term semiconductor demand.
Hyperscalers and neocloud operators face growing questions about financing, construction delays and the returns on enormous AI investments. However, semiconductor suppliers remain relatively insulated by supply shortages, particularly in memory and flash markets.
LYNX Equity Strategies said its checks into Asian memory and flash markets had not identified disruptions attributable to the US election, suggesting that underlying demand conditions remain more resilient than the stock-market reaction implies.
